name: ALG9-congenital disorder of glycosylation (ALG9-CDG, CDG type Il)

clinicalPearls: ALG9-CDG is an autosomal-recessive N-linked glycosylation defect caused by deficiency of the ALG9 alpha-1,2-mannosyltransferase, which adds specific mannose residues to the lipid-linked oligosaccharide in the endoplasmic reticulum.
Because the defect lies in assembly of the dolichol-linked precursor, it is a type I CDG and shows a type 1 transferrin isoform pattern on screening.
The neurological phenotype includes developmental delay, hypotonia and a drug-resistant epilepsy that can present as infantile spasms.
Microcephaly, failure to thrive and hepatomegaly with variable renal (cystic) and skeletal involvement are recognised features.
A severe allelic condition, Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome, is a lethal multisystem skeletal dysplasia with polycystic kidneys and cardiac and brain malformations, widening the ALG9 spectrum.
Bronchial/pericardial effusions and pericardial fluid have been reported, echoing the multisystem, protein-losing tendency seen across several CDGs.
Isoelectric focusing of transferrin is the practical first-line biochemical screen, but a normal result does not exclude CDG and genetic confirmation is required.
There is no curative therapy; unlike some other CDG subtypes ALG9-CDG is not responsive to simple oral monosaccharide supplementation, so management is supportive.
reference.pathophysiology: ALG9-CDG results from biallelic pathogenic variants in ALG9, which encodes an endoplasmic-reticulum alpha-1,2-mannosyltransferase acting in the cytosol-to-ER assembly line of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide. ALG9 catalyses the addition of specific mannose residues (adding the seventh and ninth mannose) to the growing lipid-linked oligosaccharide before it is transferred en bloc to nascent glycoproteins. Deficient activity yields a truncated, incompletely mannosylated precursor, so glycoproteins are transferred with abnormal or absent N-glycans; this defect in the assembly (rather than processing) phase defines it as a type I CDG and produces the cathodal shift of transferrin isoforms (a type 1 pattern) used diagnostically. Hypoglycosylation of numerous serum, membrane and structural glycoproteins underlies the multisystem disease, with the developing brain, liver, kidney, skeleton and serosal membranes being particularly vulnerable, explaining the encephalopathy, hepatomegaly, cystic kidneys, skeletal dysplasia and effusions across the ALG9 clinical spectrum, from the survivable neurological form to lethal Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: PMM2-CDG (the commonest type I CDG) and MPI-CDG
Other ER-assembly (ALG-family) type I CDGs such as ALG1-, ALG3-, ALG11- and ALG12-CDG
Congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathies and other secondary glycosylation defects
Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders presenting with multisystem disease and seizures
Mitochondrial disorders with multisystem involvement and developmental delay
Genetic ciliopathies/polycystic kidney disease with skeletal dysplasia (for the Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura phenotype)
Other genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (expected type 1 pattern)
Molecular confirmation by ALG9 sequencing, gene panel or exome/genome sequencing
Lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis in cultured fibroblasts (specialist confirmation of the assembly defect)
Liver function tests, coagulation profile and glycoprotein-dependent factors (e.g. antithrombin) given multisystem protein involvement
Renal ultrasound for cystic kidney disease and abdominal imaging for hepatomegaly
Brain MRI and electroencephalography for structural anomalies and seizures
Skeletal survey and cardiac evaluation, especially where a severe/lethal phenotype is suspected
redFlags: Drug-resistant seizures or infantile spasms and status epilepticus
Faltering growth with feeding failure or protein-losing state
Coagulopathy or thrombosis from hypoglycosylation of clotting regulators
Antenatal or neonatal features of a lethal skeletal dysplasia with cystic kidneys and effusions (Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura phenotype)
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and genotype-dependent: the neurological form causes significant developmental disability with epilepsy and multisystem morbidity, whereas the allelic Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome is typically lethal in the perinatal period. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, as no curative or monosaccharide-responsive treatment is established.
pitfalls: Relying on a single normal transferrin screen to exclude CDG, since results can be equivocal, especially very early in life or in mild disease.
Assuming monosaccharide therapy will help; ALG9-CDG is not among the treatable CDG subtypes such as MPI-CDG.
Overlooking coagulation and endocrine abnormalities that arise from hypoglycosylation of specific carrier and regulatory proteins.
Failing to recognise the wide phenotypic range, from a survivable encephalopathy to a lethal skeletal-renal dysplasia, when counselling families.
Not distinguishing ALG9-CDG from the more common PMM2-CDG, which changes prognosis and recurrence counselling.
